overview.summary: Greedy algorithms build up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most immediate benefit.
learningObjectives: Recognize when a locally optimal choice leads to a globally optimal solution.
Understand why Greedy algorithms often require sorting the input first.
overview.interviewRelevance: Greedy algorithms are often the O(N log N) 'trick' solutions to optimization problems that would otherwise require O(N^2) Dynamic Programming.

paragraphs: Imagine you are a cashier making change for $0.85. You want to use the fewest coins possible. You don't calculate all possible combinations of coins.

You just act 'Greedy'. You grab the biggest coin you can (a Quarter). Then another Quarter. Then another. Then a Dime. By always taking the biggest chunk possible right now, you arrive at the perfect answer.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: A Greedy algorithm never looks back. Once a choice is made, it is permanent. It never backtracks.

definition.technicalDefinition: A greedy algorithm is any algorithm that follows the problem-solving heuristic of making the locally optimal choice at each stage with the intent of finding a global optimum.

vocabulary.definition: The best possible choice you can make right now, based ONLY on the current step, ignoring future consequences.
The absolute best possible final answer for the entire problem.
A specific scenario that proves a greedy approach fails to find the global optimum.

keyProperties: Very fast (usually O(N) or O(N log N) if sorting is required).
Easy to code, incredibly hard to prove mathematically correct.
Fails if making a good choice now forces you into a terrible choice later.

metaphor: A mountain climber trying to reach the highest peak in the fog. A greedy algorithm just says 'Always step uphill'. (This works for a single mountain, but fails if there are multiple peaks).
mentalModel.clickSentence: Sort the data to reveal the most 'valuable' pieces, then gobble them up one by one until you can't.

memoryDescription: Greedy algorithms usually operate in O(1) space (excluding the sort).
They simply maintain a running total or a pointer to the current state.

memoryLayout.label: Greedy Choice
memoryLayout.value: Pick the highest value available at the current moment.

operations.name: Sort
operations.description: Most greedy problems require organizing the data first so the 'best' choices are presented first.
operations.visualNote: Items are rearranged by value or weight.

operations.name: Consume
operations.description: Iterate through the sorted data, taking whatever fits the constraints.
operations.visualNote: A pointer moves left to right, collecting items.

patternTemplate.pseudocode:
items.sort(key=custom_greedy_criteria)
result = 0
for item in items:
  if is_valid(item, current_state):
    result += item.value
    update_state()
return result
patternTemplate.whenToUse: Optimization problems (maximize profit, minimize cost) where local maximums perfectly align with the global maximum.
patternTemplate.timeComplexity: O(N log N) dominated by sorting.

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: You have a list of meeting times `[start, end]`. Find the maximum number of meetings you can attend without overlapping.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: By acting 'Greedy' and always choosing the meeting that ENDS the earliest, you leave the maximum amount of free time available for future meetings. This guarantees the optimal answer.

examples.title: Jump Game
examples.problemStatement: You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position. Return true if you can reach the last index.
steps: If your current index `i` is greater than `max_reach`, it means you are stuck. Return false.
examples.rationale: Instead of checking every possible combination of jumps (which would be O(2^N)), we greedily track the furthest possible rightward boundary we can reach.

conceptQuiz.question: Why does making change with coins (US currency) work with a Greedy algorithm, but some custom coin sets fail?
options: Because US coins (25, 10, 5, 1) are mathematically structured so that the greedy choice never 'traps' you into using more coins.
It doesn't work with US currency.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If your coins were [4, 3, 1] and you wanted to make 6. Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1 (3 coins). But the optimal answer is 3 + 3 (2 coins). Greedy fails if the coin values don't follow specific mathematical gaps.

conceptQuiz.question: If a problem can be solved by both Greedy and Dynamic Programming, which should you choose?
options: Greedy, because it is usually O(N) or O(N log N) space/time, whereas DP is often O(N^2) time/space.
Dynamic Programming, because it is safer.
They are the exact same thing.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If the Greedy Choice Property holds true, the Greedy approach will be significantly faster and use less memory than DP.

practice.title: Jump Game
practice.keyInsight: Greedily track the furthest index you can reach.

practice.title: Assign Cookies
practice.keyInsight: Sort both arrays. Give the smallest cookie to the least greedy child.

practice.title: Task Scheduler
practice.keyInsight: Always schedule the most frequent task first.
